verses.sa: अर्जुन उवाचसंन्यासस्य महाबाहो तत्त्वमिच्छामि वेदितुम् । त्यागस्य च हृषीकेश पृथक्केशिनिषूदन ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna says: O mighty-armed one, O master of the senses, O slayer of Kesi, I wish to know the distinct truth of renunciation and relinquishment.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

intro.text: The war has paused, and Arjuna stops Krishna to ask for the final distinction: what exactly is renunciation, and what is relinquishment? Listen for the difference he wants.

body.text: Arjuna says: O mighty-armed one, O master of the senses, O slayer of Kesi, I wish to know the distinct truth of renunciation and relinquishment. Arjuna asks to know the distinct truth of sannyasa and tyaga separately. He does not ask for new rules, but for the exact border between two ways of giving up. Krishna answers by defining sannyasa as giving up desire-born actions, and tyaga as giving up the results of all actions.

verses.sa: श्री भगवानुवाचकाम्यानां कर्मणां न्यासं संन्यासं कवयो विदुः । सर्वकर्मफलत्यागं प्राहुस्त्यागं विचक्षणाः ॥
verses.tr: The wise call renunciation the giving up of desire-born actions. The discerning call renunciation the giving up of all results of action.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna answers Arjuna’s question by naming two kinds of renunciation, then defines each one.

body.text: The wise call renunciation the giving up of desire-born actions. The discerning call renunciation the giving up of all results of action. Krishna gives two definitions in this verse. The wise call renunciation the giving up of desire-born actions, while the discerning call it the giving up of all results of action. Krishna now warns against the extreme view that all action should be abandoned as flawed.

verses.sa: त्याज्यं दोषवदित्येके कर्म प्राहुर्मनीषिणः । यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यमिति चापरे ॥
verses.tr: Some wise people say all action should be abandoned as flawed. Others say sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned.
verses.angle: Two camps of the wise on action
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's final question about letting go by showing that even the wise cannot agree. Listen for the two camps.

body.text: Some wise people say all action should be abandoned as flawed. Others say sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned. Here are two camps of the wise, and Krishna does not yet take a side. One camp says action itself is flawed and must be abandoned. The other camp says sacrifice, giving, and austerity must never be abandoned. Krishna now steps in to give his own settled view on what true renunciation actually is.

verses.sa: निश्चयं श्रृणु मे तत्र त्यागे भरतसत्तम । त्यागो हि पुरुषव्याघ्र त्रिविधः संप्रकीर्तितः ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna, first hear my settled view on renunciation. Renunciation is said to be threefold.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna pauses to settle the debate between action and withdrawal. He tells Arjuna to listen to his settled view on renunciation.

body.text: Arjuna, first hear my settled view on renunciation. Renunciation is said to be threefold. Krishna calls Arjuna bharatasattama, best of the Bharatas, to honor him before giving this final teaching, and immediately adds that tyaga, renunciation, is threefold, so the path forward must be understood with precision. Sanjaya will soon describe how the armies stand arrayed, ready for the war to begin. Listen for the first sounds of the battle.

verses.sa: यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यं कार्यमेव तत् । यज्ञो दानं तपश्चैव पावनानि मनीषिणाम् ॥
verses.tr: Sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned; they must be done. These three actions purify thoughtful people.
verses.angle: Yajna, dana and tapas purify the wise
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for three actions that Krishna says are purifying, and that even the wise should never abandon.

body.text: Sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned; they must be done. These three actions purify thoughtful people. Krishna names three actions, yajna, dana, and tapas, and says they purify thoughtful people. He does not drop them from duty, but places them at the heart of it. Krishna then says these same actions must be done without attachment, without wanting their results.

verses.sa: एतान्यपि तु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा फलानि च । कर्तव्यानीति मे पार्थ निश्िचतं मतमुत्तमम् ॥
verses.tr: Even these actions, and all other actions, should be done without attachment and without wanting their results. This is my settled and best teaching, O Arjuna.
verses.angle: Niscitam matam uttamam, settled best opinion
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now gives Arjuna the final word on how to act, making his teaching on sacred duty absolutely clear.

body.text: Even these actions, and all other actions, should be done without attachment and without wanting their results. This is my settled and best teaching, O Arjuna. Krishna calls this his settled, best opinion. He tells Partha that even these actions, meaning all duties including sacrifice and discipline, must be done without attachment and without wanting the results. Krishna warns that giving up prescribed action in confusion is a tamasic way to live. Listen to why he says that.

verses.sa: नियतस्य तु संन्यासः कर्मणो नोपपद्यते । मोहात्तस्य परित्यागस्तामसः परिकीर्तितः ॥
verses.tr: Abandoning prescribed action is not right. Giving it up in confusion is called tamasic.
verses.angle: tamasah: the dark kind of giving up
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just told you to keep acting without attachment. Now he warns against a specific trap.

body.text: Abandoning prescribed action is not right. Giving it up in confusion is called tamasic. Krishna names the exact kind of renunciation he rejects: tamasah, the dark or dull kind. It is not the action itself that is wrong, but the confusion, moha, that makes a man drop his duty. Krishna now says that renouncing action out of fear of pain is a passionate failure that yields no fruit.

verses.sa: दुःखमित्येव यत्कर्म कायक्लेशभयात्त्यजेत् । स कृत्वा राजसं त्यागं नैव त्यागफलं लभेत् ॥
verses.tr: If someone gives up action thinking it is only suffering and fearing bodily strain, that renunciation is passionate, and it brings no fruit of renunciation.
verses.angle: Rajasa tyaga: the passionate giving up
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has been sorting the different kinds of giving up. Listen to the one that looks like peace but is actually fear.

body.text: If someone gives up action thinking it is only suffering and fearing bodily strain, that renunciation is passionate, and it brings no fruit of renunciation. Krishna calls this kind of giving up rajasa, passionate. It is not the calm of true release, but the restless recoil of someone who steps back from their duty simply because it hurts. Krishna now turns to the giving up that is done without clinging to results, the true sattvic path.

verses.sa: कार्यमित्येव यत्कर्म नियतं क्रियतेऽर्जुन । सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा फलं चैव स त्यागः सात्त्विको मतः ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna, when fixed duty is done as only duty, without clinging to results, that renunciation is called sattvic.
verses.angle: Sattvic tyaga: doing work without attachment or fruit
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now teaches the cleanest form of letting go. Listen to how he defines the highest sacrifice.

body.text: Arjuna, when fixed duty is done as only duty, without clinging to results, that renunciation is called sattvic. Krishna calls it sattvic tyaga, giving up both attachment and fruit at once, so the action is done purely because it is required. Krishna then speaks of the wise renunciate who neither rejects unwholesome action nor clings to wholesome action.

verses.sa: न द्वेष्ट्यकुशलं कर्म कुशले नानुषज्जते । त्यागी सत्त्वसमाविष्टो मेधावी छिन्नसंशयः ॥
verses.tr: One who neither rejects unwholesome action nor clings to wholesome action is a wise renunciate, free of doubt and established in clear seeing.
verses.angle: Anushajjate: the wise do not cling to good works
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for one verb. It shows how a wise person acts without attachment to results.

body.text: One who neither rejects unwholesome action nor clings to wholesome action is a wise renunciate, free of doubt and established in clear seeing. Listen for one verb, anushajjate, clings to. The wise one does not cling to wholesome action, the very thing most people chase. This is how a renunciate acts. Krishna now explains why total renunciation is impossible for any embodied being.

verses.sa: न हि देहभृता शक्यं त्यक्तुं कर्माण्यशेषतः । यस्तु कर्मफलत्यागी स त्यागीत्यभिधीयते ॥
verses.tr: For embodied beings, total renunciation of action is impossible. Therefore, one who renounces the fruits of action is called a renunciant.
verses.angle: Dehbhrita: one who bears a body, cannot give up action
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna answers the question of how to truly give up. He points to the one who bears a body and the one who gives up the fruit.

body.text: For embodied beings, total renunciation of action is impossible. Therefore, one who renounces the fruits of action is called a renunciant. The verse turns on one word, karmaphalatyagi, the renouncer of the fruit. Krishna says the one who drops the reward while the action stays on is the true renunciant. The next verse explains the three results for those who cling to the fruit, and the freedom of those who do not.

verses.sa: अनिष्टमिष्टं मिश्रं च त्रिविधं कर्मणः फलम् । भवत्यत्यागिनां प्रेत्य न तु संन्यासिनां क्वचित् ॥
verses.tr: For those who do not renounce the fruits of action, action produces three kinds of results, pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed, even after death; but for those who renounce the fruits, there is no such result anywhere.
verses.angle: Trividham: the threefold fruits of action
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now answers the question of what happens to those who still expect results. Listen for the threefold fruit of action.

body.text: For those who do not renounce the fruits of action, action produces three kinds of results, pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed, even after death; but for those who renounce the fruits, there is no such result anywhere. Krishna names the three kinds of fruit: pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed. These three results continue for those who cling to outcomes even after death. Krishna then tells Arjuna to learn the five causes behind all actions.

verses.sa: पञ्चैतानि महाबाहो कारणानि निबोध मे । सांख्ये कृतान्ते प्रोक्तानि सिद्धये सर्वकर्मणाम् ॥
verses.tr: O mighty-armed one, learn from Me these five causes, taught in the Sankhya system, for the accomplishment of all actions.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to understand that every action depends on five causes, and not on one person deciding to do it alone. Listen for the five causes.

body.text: O mighty-armed one, learn from Me these five causes, taught in the Sankhya system, for the accomplishment of all actions. The text says these five causes are taught in Sankhya, a philosophy of knowledge. Krishna cites it to show that human action is not as simple as one person deciding and doing everything alone. Krishna names the five factors, starting with the field, the doer, and the instruments.

verses.sa: अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् । विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥
verses.tr: The field, the doer, the instruments, the many efforts, and the fifth factor, the unseen force, all shape every action.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna now breaks every action into its hidden parts, showing that no one acts alone. Listen for the five causes he lists.

body.text: The field, the doer, the instruments, the many efforts, and the fifth factor, the unseen force, all shape every action. The verse names five factors, and the fifth is daivam, the unseen force. This shows that behind every deed stands a power beyond the doer. Krishna then says that whatever a person does, right or wrong, carries these same five causes.
